claims.text: Low hardness and strength in equimolar or near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi are governed by low lattice friction and weak obstacles to dislocation motion.
The alloy has a relatively small local atomic-size mismatch.
The alloy lacks significant short-range chemical order.
The simple solid-solution state lacks second phases and nanoscale precipitates.
Small atomic-size mismatch and the absence of short-range order or precipitates permit easy dislocation nucleation and glide.
Small atomic-size mismatch and the absence of short-range order or precipitates promote dynamic recovery during deformation.
The solid solution has uniform, minimally distorted atomic arrangements and low local lattice distortion.
Low lattice distortion and negligible short-range ordering produce sparse dislocation pinning and weak forest hardening.
Atomic-radius differences among Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, and Ti are insufficient in this solid solution to generate strong local lattice strains.
Dislocation annihilation and rearrangement through dynamic recovery lead to low work hardening.
Low work hardening limits hardness and yield strength while retaining high plasticity and machinability.
Mechanical testing will show relatively low yield strength and hardness together with extensive plastic deformation.
In situ characterization will reveal a high density of mobile dislocations with limited entanglement or pile-up.
A comparable alloy with enhanced lattice distortion will exhibit a higher work-hardening rate than the starting CoCrFeNiTi state.
CoCrFeNi without Ti typically has higher hardness and strength because of more effective dislocation pinning.
Adding a larger microalloying atom in small quantities will increase lattice distortion.
Increasing lattice distortion should increase dislocation pinning and measurable hardening.
Secondary phases, precipitates, or deformation-induced phase transformations would independently increase hardness and strength.
The hypothesis is restricted to single-phase CoCrFeNiTi under ambient or moderately varying temperatures and strain rates without deformation-induced phase transformation.
